name: Kyphi
description: Kyphi was the sacred evening incense of ancient Egypt, recorded on the temple walls of Edfu and Philae and later described by Plutarch and Dioscorides. It was compounded over many days from resins, spices and roots kneaded with wine, honey and raisins, and was said to lull the senses and bring vivid dreams. This simplified home version keeps the essential structure of the classic recipes.
steps: Soak the chopped raisins in just enough red wine to cover overnight.
Grind the resins to a coarse powder, then grind the cinnamon, juniper, cardamom, lemongrass and sandalwood together.
Mash the wine-soaked raisins into a paste and warm with the honey gently until runny.
Knead the dry powders into the raisin-honey paste until it forms a stiff, sticky dough, adding more wine or powder as needed.
Roll the dough into pea-sized pellets and set them on parchment to dry in a warm, airy place for 1 to 2 weeks.
Store in a glass jar and cure for at least a month; traditional kyphi improves for a year or more.
howToUse: Light a charcoal disc with tongs and wait until it is fully ashed over and glowing (about 5 minutes). Sprinkle a pinch (1/4 teaspoon) of incense onto it, adding more as the smoke fades. Place one kyphi pellet at a time on the coal. Burn at dusk to honor the gods, before sleep for dreaming, or during meditation and temple-style devotion.
chant: Breath of Ra at setting sun, resin, wine and honey spun; open gates of dream and night, guide my spirit in your light.
intention: I enter the sacred stillness of the temple and the world of dreams.
timing: Sunset; full moon; any evening devotion.
caution: Burn only on a charcoal disc handled with tongs, in a heatproof censer filled with sand or salt, on a stable surface away from curtains, paper, hair and sleeves; never leave it unattended or fall asleep while it burns, and let used charcoal cool completely (several hours, or douse it in water) before disposal. Burning charcoal gives off carbon monoxide, so burn only in a well-ventilated room with a window open (never in a closed room, tent or vehicle), keep working smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, and get to fresh air if you feel a headache, dizziness or nausea. Incense smoke irritates the lungs: avoid it if you have asthma, COPD or another breathing condition, and keep it away from pregnant people, infants and young children. Keep birds out of the area entirely (their lungs are extremely sensitive to smoke), let other pets leave the room, and store the loose blend where children and pets cannot reach it; never eat or drink it. Pellets contain sugar and may flare, so burn one at a time, and keep them away from dogs, because raisins can cause kidney failure in dogs.
pets: Smoke is dangerous to birds and irritates cats' and dogs' airways: keep birds well away in a closed-off room and let pets leave. Keep the loose blend from pets, since raisins (kidney failure in dogs) and lemongrass are toxic to them if eaten.

name: Temple Incense
description: A classic general-purpose ritual incense in the Wiccan and ceremonial tradition, used to sanctify the circle and lift the mind toward the sacred. Frankincense and myrrh, the incense of temples from Jerusalem to Rome, are rounded with benzoin and a little sandalwood.
steps: Cleanse your mortar and pestle and mixing bowl, then set out each ingredient and measure by parts (1 part can be a teaspoon for a small batch or a tablespoon for a jar).
Grind the resins first, alone, into a coarse powder; chill them in the freezer for 10 minutes beforehand if they are sticky.
Grind the woods, barks and seeds next, then crumble the leaves and flowers by hand so they keep some texture.
Add the frankincense essential oil drop by drop to the ground resins and stir to distribute.
Combine everything in the bowl, mixing clockwise with your fingers or a wooden spoon while speaking the chant and holding your intention.
Store in a labeled, airtight glass jar in a dark place and let it cure for 2 weeks before burning so the scents meld.
howToUse: Light a charcoal disc with tongs and wait until it is fully ashed over and glowing (about 5 minutes). Sprinkle a pinch (1/4 teaspoon) of incense onto it, adding more as the smoke fades. Burn at the start of any ritual to sanctify the space, during meditation and prayer, or to consecrate altar tools by passing them through the smoke.
chant: Rise, O smoke, to realms above, carry prayer and carry love; holy is this sacred space, fill it now with light and grace.
intention: This space is made sacred and my spirit lifted.
timing: Any time; especially Sunday or the full moon.

Keep birds out of the area entirely (their lungs are extremely sensitive to smoke), let other pets leave the room, and store the loose blend where children and pets cannot reach it; never eat or drink it. The added essential oil makes the blend more flammable, so use only the drops given.
pets: Smoke is dangerous to birds and irritates cats' and dogs' airways: keep birds well away in a closed-off room and let pets leave.
